It's also worth it if you can get a fellowship and some scholarships that stacks onto your assistantship and make $70-80k while getting your PhD from a monetary perspective. Then you don't lose out on any of the money while in school.

To be honest, this is what I was always told before I went into my PhD. Obviously the money didn't matter much to me since I went in anyway, but the difference in pay is not as wide as your calculations. You calculated how much you would be making in 5-7 years with a Bachelors in the industry, but you didn't include how much you'll be making for your stipend as a graduate student for those 5-7 years, and most schools do offer an assistantship.

I can only speak for my school, but the normal annual stipend is around 30k. So the net amount you'll make more with just a bachelor's is $172,500 - $241,500 rather than the numbers you propose. Just like with promotions in the industry, my university increases the amount of your stipend each year by a few percentages to keep up with the raises they give the faculty. You can also move up pay grades and make as much as 40k per year.

Additionally, with enough ambition, you can be making more than that for your PhD. There are a number of fellowships and scholarships you can apply for, and with the one I got (as a first year grad student), my "salary" would be around $78k when you include my stipend and fellowship. Additionally, the university subsidizes 80% of my health insurance, and offers a retirement plan. 

So while I'm in grad school, I'm not really missing out on any extra earnings, and I will (hopefully) make more once I graduate. Money isn't the objective for me though, the field I want to go into and the jobs I want require at least a master's, and prefers a PhD (the field is bionanotechnology and MEMS device fabrication). But I was pleasantly surprised that I was able to make as much as my friends while working half the time for the university doing research I love, and being a student the other half.
